Hi Chris / Rebecca —

Thanks for the clear questions. Technical answers below — happy to expand these in the workshop and during an in-house load test.

1) Scale-up times- Cold start (new GPU instance boot + model load): typically 90–180s depending on model size and region.
- Warm pool (pre-initialized instances with model loaded, idle KV cache): ~10–30s to start serving requests (depends on model quantization and warm pool size).
- Fast-path pre-warmed sessions (reserved slots with cached KV): sub-10s first-response possible for short sessions.

2) Warm pools & burst capacity- We recommend a hybrid approach: maintain a small warm pool sized to absorb typical bursts (say 10–20% of expected burst concurrency). For RetailAI's burst pattern (1,200 concurrent), we'd size warm pool to handle ~200–300 requests instantly and autoscale the rest.
- Warm pools are billed as part of reserved/dedicated capacity if you opt for Dedicated; on Hosted we can configure ephemeral warm instances billed as usage with a small warm-pool premium.

3) Queueing and admission control- Redwood supports configurable admission policies:
  • Soft queue (bounded): requests queue for a short window (e.g., 5–15s) while autoscaling catches up; client receives progress/ETA headers.
  • Hard reject: when queue depth exceeds threshold, requests are rejected with a 429 + Retry-After.
  • Prioritized lanes: streaming interactive sessions can be given higher priority than batch jobs.

Recommendation: use soft queue with short TTL plus client-side retry/backoff for best UX. We can also front-load small prewarm bursts during known peak windows.

4) Streaming & first-token latency- Streaming prioritizes first-token latency. We split work: immediate lightweight token generation path (fast attention kernels) to deliver first token, then batch subsequent tokens. That helps p95 first-token under moderate concurrency. Under very large spikes the warm pool + admission control determine first-token behavior.

5) Concurrency & throughput guidance- Per-GPU concurrency depends on model family and quantization. Example: for a 8-bit quantized Llama-2-13B-ish variant, one GPU typically supports ~40–60 concurrent interactive sessions with acceptable latencies; for larger families you’ll need more GPUs or smaller model variants. We’ll run a quick capacity estimate in the workshop against your average tokens/request.

6) Recommended deployment for strict SLOs- For predictable p95 SLOs during high bursts we recommend Dedicated reserved capacity (guaranteed warm pool + SLA). Hosted + warm pools can work but will have higher variance and potential cold-start tails unless you commit to a larger warm pool or useReservations.

Next steps I can own:
- Attach a short autoscale primer and the SLO spreadsheet (attached).
- Propose warm-pool sizing scenarios based on the SLO worksheet you fill out.
- Schedule a 60m technical workshop + load-test plan.
